svg.title: The Stupp regimen on a timeline: six concomitant weeks, a break, six maintenance cycles
svg.desc: Schematic timeline of the standard glioblastoma course (the Stupp regimen), in three parts. The top strip is drawn to scale and shows the shape of the whole course: after surgery come phase 1, the six concomitant weeks; phase 2, a break of 2 to 6 weeks; and phase 3, maintenance, six cycles of 28 days each. The interval between surgery and radiotherapy is annotated: the data support starting within six weeks with no detectable effect on survival, which is not the same as the sooner the better. The middle panel enlarges the six concomitant weeks, one box per day across 42 days: the radiotherapy row is filled only Monday to Friday, 30 boxes in all, labelled 2 Gy times 30 fractions equals 60 Gy; the temozolomide row is filled on all seven days including weekends, with the protocol dose of 75 mg/m². The step between the two rows at the weekend is the teaching point of the figure. The lower panel enlarges maintenance: six cycles side by side, 28 days each, with only the first 5 days carrying the drug and the other 23 days not, at the protocol dose of 150 to 200 mg/m². A block of text on the figure states that these are the doses written into the randomised trial protocol, that they are not your prescription and not a dose table to check yourself against, that your team calculates your dose, and that you should not stop or add doses on your own. Two side cards carry the Taiwan material: clause 9.25 of the National Health Insurance drug reimbursement rules requires prior authorisation, limits each authorised course to three months, and requires objective evidence such as imaging of no progression before the next course, so the real pacemaker is a three-monthly gate with imaging attached and the clause contains no mention of six months; and extending to 12 cycles gives slightly better progression-free survival, the same overall survival and more side effects. The figure shows no survival times of any kind.

g.text: THE STUPP REGIMEN, LAID OUT IN DAYS
Six weeks together, a break, then six cycles
Radiotherapy runs Monday to Friday; temozolomide is taken every day of the week, weekends included. The gap between those
two rows is what this figure is for.
The doses shown are the ones written into the trial protocol. They are not your prescription — your team works that out.
The shape of the whole course (this strip is drawn to scale)
Surgery
1 Concomitant phase
2 Break | 2–6 weeks
3 Maintenance | six cycles (28 days each)
six weeks
Surgery to the start of radiotherapy: the data support starting within six weeks, with no detectable effect on survival — which is not the same as "the sooner the better"
The two panels below are enlargements; their lengths are not to scale.
Phase 1, the six concomitant weeks, day by day
Week 1
Week 2
Week 3
Week 4
Week 5
Week 6
Radiotherapy
once a day, Monday to Friday; 2 Gy × 30 fractions = 60 Gy
Temozolomide
every day of the week, weekends included; the protocol says 75 mg/m²
Weekends: radiotherapy stops, the drug does not
Phase 3, maintenance: six cycles of 28 days
Cycle 1
Cycle 2

Cycle 6
Only the first 5 days of each cycle carry the drug (the darker block); the other 23 days do not. The protocol says 150–200 mg/m².
About the mg figures on this page
These are the doses written into the randomised trial protocol, shown so that the shape of the course makes sense. They are not your prescription and not a dose table
to check yourself against — your team calculates your dose from body surface area, blood counts and liver and kidney function. Do not stop or add doses on your own.
How Taiwan's NHI reimbursement paces this (drug reimbursement rules, clause 9.25)
The clause requires prior authorisation before use, limits each authorised course to three months,
and requires objective evidence (imaging, for example) of no progression before the next course is
granted. So the real pacemaker is a three-monthly gate with imaging attached — the clause contains
no mention of "six months".
"Can I take it for a few more months?"
Extending to 12 cycles: progression-free survival is slightly better,
overall survival is the same, and there are more side effects. This
figure draws only the six cycles of the protocol.
Schematic, redrawn from the treatment protocol of Stupp 2005, Stupp 2009, the pooled analysis of extended cycles and GEINO 14-01, together with clause 9.25 of
the National Health Insurance Administration drug reimbursement rules (Taiwan); the cohorts, designs and endpoints of the underlying studies differ, so the data
points must not be compared directly.
